abstract: Faces provide the most diagnostic information for identifying individuals in humans. Understanding the neural mechanisms involved in face identity recognition (FIR) is particularly important for unfamiliar faces, for which identity cannot rely on encoded multimodal semantic associations. Here, we investigated the neural basis of FIR using an original frequency-tagging fMRI approach providing objective, sensitive, and reliable measures of face recognition. Ten human participants were presented within a rapid 6 Hz stream of natural images of a single unfamiliar identity in two conditions: (1) with the same face image across low-level changes (size, luminance, contrast) only, or (2) with images varying in background, size, head orientation, gaze direction, etc. Every 9 s during a 243 s run, seven images of different unfamiliar identities were introduced in bursts. For each participant and each condition, we recorded runs with upright and inverted faces. Analyses were performed within face-selective regions (defined from a frequency-tagging localizer) and in the Fourier domain, where individual face discrimination responses were objectively identified and quantified at the identity-change frequency (0.111 Hz). We observed robust image-based individual face discrimination responses across both conditions in core face-selective ventral regions (LatMidFG and IOG). In contrast, responses in early visual cortex and the pSTS were negligible in our second condition, which required generalization across viewpoint variations. In addition, the LatMidFG showed a reliable inversion effect, confirming that the observed responses cannot be attributed solely to low-level image differences. Overall, these findings highlight the value of fMRI frequency-tagging for objectively characterizing the cortical network underlying unfamiliar FIR, providing evidence for high-level discrimination and generalization of unfamiliar face identity in the human ventral occipito-temporal face-selective network.
